newsitem.title: TAIWAN: King of China noodles mulls huge return to Taiwan.
newsitem.headline: King of China noodles mulls huge return to Taiwan.

text.p: Taiwan's Hong Kong-listed Tingyi (Cayman Islands) Holding Corp, which dominates the mainland China instant noodle market, said on Friday it was considering a T$10 billion investment at home in Taiwan.

"We have begun considering bringing some investment back to Taiwan, but we have no concrete plan yet," Chen Tsai-chun, vice president of Tingyi's unlisted Taiwan parent Ting Hsin Oil and Fat International Co, told Reuters by Telephone.
"Ten billion Taiwan dollars is our initial investment target," Chen said.
Tingyi, with annual China sales that Chen put at T$20 billion, has come to dominate the mainland's fast-growing instant noodle market with its popular Kang Shifu brand.
Chen indicated that Tingyi wanted to comply with a Taiwan government call for local enterprises to consider reinvesting in Taiwan rather than the rival Chinese communist mainland.

"We are happy to have the opportunity and ability to return to Taiwan and hope the government can seriously consider our plan," Chen said without elaborating on what role he expected the state to play.

"The priority of our overseas investment is to make money, but we get a homey feeling by coming back to our hometown," he added. "Aside from just seeking profitable projects, we hope our investments can benefit the local economy."
Taiwan, which has banned direct links with China since a civil war split them in 1949, has allowed a range of "indirect" investments under a political thaw dating to the late 1980s.
It was this opportunity that took Tingyi to the mainland, along with some 30,000 other firms that collectively have poured more than US$30 billion into China.

Things turned sour in mid-1995 when Beijing froze what had been slowly warming semi-official contacts with Taipei, prompting the Nationalist government to grow more cautious about its policy on investment in the Chinese mainland.

In May, Taiwan banned investment in mainland infrastructure -- chiefly water works, railways, harbours, airports, roads and power plants -- to avoid the political vulnerability that could come with becoming overdependent on its rival's huge economy.

At the same time, however, Taipei lifted restrictions on more than 400 categories of mainland investment, including travel agencies, hotels, recreation facilities, warehouses, merchandise agents, rental businesses, saunas, printing machines, sewing machines and car and motorcycle parts.
Some 4,350 investment types now are permitted.
